title: Strozzapreti al Ragù
subtitle: hand-rolled pasta with slow-cooked meat ragu
excerpt: Strozzapreti al ragù pairs hand-rolled pasta twists with a slow-cooked meat sauce of beef and pork mince, red wine, tomatoes and soffritto. The pasta is made from just flour and water with no eggs, giving it a firm, slightly chewy texture that holds the thick ragù well. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Strozzapreti, meaning priest stranglers, is a hand-rolled pasta from Emilia-Romagna and the surrounding regions. The name is the subject of much folklore, most versions involving clergy and overeating. The pasta is made by rolling small pieces of dough against the palm of the hand to create twisted, hollow tubes that catch thick sauces like ragù.

recipe.freezeNotes: The ragù freezes well for up to 3 months. The fresh pasta does not freeze well once rolled.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a double batch of ragù and freeze half.

glossaryTerms.definition: A hand-rolled pasta from Emilia-Romagna made from flour and water, twisted into short irregular tubes. The name means priest stranglers.
An Italian meat sauce slow-cooked with wine, tomatoes and soffritto until rich and thick. The Bolognese is the most internationally famous version.

content.text: is a two-part project: the pasta and the meat sauce cook separately and come together only at the end. The

are shaped by pressing and rolling a small rectangle of dough against your palm, creating an irregular twist that holds sauce in its folds. The ragù needs a minimum of two hours to develop its depth. Serves 4.
Start the ragù first, then make the pasta while it simmers. The pasta takes about 40 minutes to mix, rest and shape, which fits neatly into the ragù's cooking time.
Start the ragù: heat the olive oil in a heavy-based pan over medium heat. Add the onion, carrot and celery and cook for 10 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and cook for another minute.
Add the beef and pork mince. Break them up and cook, stirring, for 8 minutes until browned all over. Season to taste.

Pour in the red wine. Let it bubble for 2 minutes until mostly evaporated. Add the tinned tomatoes and break them up with a spoon. Add a splash of water to rinse the can. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover loosely and cook for 2 hours, stirring occasionally. Add a splash of water if it gets too thick.

Make the pasta: tip the flour onto a clean surface. Make a well in the centre and gradually add the warm water, mixing with a fork, then your hands, until a rough dough forms. Knead for 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Wrap and rest for 30 minutes.

Divide the pasta dough into four portions. Roll each to about 2mm thick. Cut into rectangles roughly 3cm by 5cm. Press each rectangle against your palm and roll it away from you with your other hand to create a twisted tube shape. Set on a floured tray.
Bring a large pot of water to the boil. Cook the strozzapreti in batches for 2 to 3 minutes until they float and are just cooked through. Drain, reserving a cup of pasta water.
Taste and adjust the ragù seasoning. Add the drained pasta to the ragù and toss over low heat for 1 minute, adding a splash of pasta water if needed. Serve with grated parmesan.

attrs.symptom: Pasta dough is too stiff to roll
attrs.cause: Not enough water was added or the flour absorbed it unevenly
attrs.fix: Add water a tablespoon at a time, kneading between additions. The dough should feel firm but pliable, like Play-Doh

attrs.cause: The fat from the mince was not absorbed into the sauce
attrs.fix: Skim the surface fat with a spoon, or stir in a splash of pasta water which will help emulsify the fat back into the sauce

attrs.cause: They were not rolled tightly enough or the dough was too soft
attrs.fix: Press the dough firmly as you roll each piece and make sure it is well rested before shaping

content.text: Strozzapreti comes from Emilia-Romagna and is also common in Tuscany and Umbria. Different regions claim the pasta and argue about the correct shape. The ragù partner changes by area too, from the milk-softened Bolognese in the north to richer, redder sauces further south. This version sits in the middle: a straightforward meat sauce that takes time but very little skill.
